bread-french-or-vienna-whole-wheat.title: Bread, French or Vienna, whole wheat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole‑wheat French or Vienna bread is made from whole wheat flour, a natural sourdough starter, and a modest amount of salt. It features a crisp crust, aromatic crumb, and a subtle tang typical of sourdough breads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional French (baguette) and Viennese loaves are often baked in steam ovens, giving them a crunchy crust.
Whole‑wheat flour retains the bran and germ, making the bread more nutritious than white flour breads.
The sourdough starter contains live lactic‑acid bacteria that enhance flavor and extend shelf life.
In France and Austria, bread is a cultural staple and is served with virtually every meal.
Whole‑wheat bread has a lower glycemic index than white bread because carbohydrates are released more slowly.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑wheat bread provides dietary fiber that supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Whole grains supply iron, magnesium, and zinc, important for blood formation and immune support.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Live cultures from the sourdough can help foster beneficial bacteria in the intestine.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact
items.content: Compared with white bread, whole‑wheat varieties cause a slower rise in blood sugar levels.

items.title: Wheat allergy or celiac disease
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease should avoid this bread as it can trigger adverse reactions.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some recipes contain a noticeable amount of salt; individuals monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While healthier than white bread, it still provides calories; portion control is advisable for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bread works well for sandwiches, toast, serving alongside soups and salads, or as a base for bruschetta. It can be toasted, used for croutons, breadcrumb coating, or as an open‑face snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the loaf in a paper bag or linen cloth at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag – it retains flavor and texture for up to 2 months. Thaw and warm in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Breadsticks are crunchy, hard crackers made from whole‑wheat flour. They have a rich, nutty flavor, a dense texture, and are often enjoyed as a snack or accompaniment to soups and salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑wheat breadsticks retain bran and germ, making them more nutritious than white crackers.
Their hard texture allows them to stay crisp for a long time without becoming stale.
In some countries they are served with olive oil and spices as a wine‑pairing appetizer.
Traditionally they are baked as long thin sticks and then cut into bite‑size pieces.
Variants with sunflower, pumpkin or flax seeds add extra flavor and health benefits.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑wheat flour preserves a high amount of fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3 and B6 vitamins help with energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Breadsticks provide magnesium, iron and zinc, important for muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Absence of added sugars makes them suitable for moderate consumption when monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of fiber and complex carbs helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Some varieties are salted; people with hypertension should choose unsalted versions.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Made from wheat, they are not suitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although not sweet, dense crackers can add up in calories if eaten in large portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breadsticks can be eaten straight as a snack, dipped in sauces, added to salads for crunch, or served alongside soups. They are also used in cooking to make breadcrumb coatings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness and prevent mold.

burrito-bowl-beef-or-pork-with-rice.title: Burrito Bowl, Beef or Pork, with Rice

content.title: About
content.content: The burrito bowl is a Mexican‑inspired dish served in a bowl with rice, beans, vegetables and a choice of meat (beef or pork). It is finished with salsa, guacamole and sour cream, offering a balanced flavor and a nutritious combination.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bowl version was created as a lighter alternative to the traditional wrapped burrito.
Original recipes often use brown rice, which retains more nutrients than white rice.
Meat is typically marinated in chipotle spices, giving it a subtle smoky note.
The dish is popular across the US and Canada as a quick‑service lunch option.
Beef is usually taken from a lean cut, while pork uses tenderloin to keep fat content moderate.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef and pork provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice, especially whole‑grain, supplies slowly digestible energy and helps maintain stable blood sugar.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat and rice deliver niacin, vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Vegetable content
items.content: Added veggies (tomatoes, corn, lettuce) add fiber, vitamins and antioxidants.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sauces and seasonings can add a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Both beef and pork can contain saturated fats; choosing lean cuts is advisable.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: If a sauce contains wheat flour, it may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking of meat can allow pathogenic bacteria to grow.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the burrito bowl in a deep dish. Toss all ingredients together, add sauce to taste, and enjoy with a fork or spoon. A squeeze of fresh lime, cilantro, or crunchy tortilla chips can be added for extra texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: If prepared ahead, keep the bowl in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat rice and meat to an internal temperature of 75 °C, adding fresh vegetables just before serving.

corned-beef-sandwich-on-wheat-with-chees.title: Corned Beef Sandwich on Wheat with Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A corned beef and cheese sandwich served on a slice of wheat bread is a hearty, flavorful snack. The corned beef is made from brisket cured in a seasoned brine, while the cheese adds a creamy note.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corned beef is traditionally associated with Irish cuisine and is popular on St. Patrick's Day.
Wheat bread provides slow‑release carbohydrates that help maintain energy levels.
The sandwich is convenient for on‑the‑go meals, often found in school cafeterias and picnics.
The salty beef and mellow cheese create a sweet‑salty, creamy flavor balance.
Original recipes cure the beef with mustard, cloves, and bay leaf.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Corned beef supplies high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese adds calcium important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Energy‑dense carbs
items.content: Wheat bread offers complex carbohydrates that promote lasting satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and bread contain B1, B3, and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Corned beef is often cured with a lot of salt, which can be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese and meat can increase saturated fat intake, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with dairy allergies or lactose intolerance.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which should be avoided by people with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be enjoyed hot, lightly toasted on a grill or toaster, or cold. Slice it in half for kids or serve whole for adults. Add lettuce, tomato, or mustard for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Unopened corned beef can be stored at room temperature until the date printed on the package.

green-beans-fresh-cooked-with-butter-or-.title: Green beans, fresh, cooked with butter or margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Green beans are young pods of the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) harvested before the seeds fully mature. When cooked with butter or margarine, they retain a crisp texture and acquire a delicate, buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans are a good source of B‑vitamins, vitamin C, and potassium.
Cooking them with fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble nutrients.
They are known as "green beans" in the US and "haricots verts" in France.
The French‑style bean is a thinner variety prized for its tenderness.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 35 kcal, making it suitable for weight management.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vitamin C, vitamin K, and folate contribute to immune function, blood clotting, and cell health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure, and plant compounds can lower cholesterol.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to beans.

items.title: Food poisoning risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked beans may contain phytohemagglutinin, which can cause gastrointestinal upset.

items.title: Sodium content in added fats
items.content: When using salted butter or margarine, monitor sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steam or sauté the beans in a small amount of butter or margarine until tender but still crisp. Season with salt, pepper, and a squeeze of lemon. Serve as a side dish with meat, fish, or tossed into salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh beans in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or container for 3‑5 days. Cooked beans can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Lo mein is a classic Chinese stir‑fried noodle dish made from wheat flour noodles. This version features tender strips of pork, mixed vegetables, and a savory soy‑based sauce, creating a flavorful and satisfying meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lo mein originated in China in the early 20th century as a popular street‑food dish.
Traditionally the noodles are hand‑pulled, but most modern restaurants use pre‑made dried noodles for convenience.
Pork is usually sliced thin and quickly stir‑fried to stay juicy.
The dish is often garnished with scallions, carrots, and bean sprouts for added texture and taste.
A Japanese counterpart called “yaki udon” uses a sweeter sauce but follows a similar preparation method.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Both pork and wheat noodles provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Pork supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: Noodles deliver quick‑release carbs, making the meal a good pre‑exercise option.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Added vegetables such as carrots and bean sprouts provide vitamins A and C and other antioxidants.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can be very salty; people with hypertension should limit the amount used.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat noodles contain gluten, making the dish unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Pork fat
items.content: Some cuts of pork are fatty; choosing lean cuts or trimming excess fat reduces saturated fat intake.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy should substitute the sauce with a soy‑free alternative.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve lo mein hot, tossing the noodles with sauce and pork. It is typically eaten with a fork or chopsticks, cutting larger pork pieces as needed. A squeeze of lime or a sprinkle of fresh cilantro adds brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best enjoyed immediately. If leftovers are needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat with a splash of water or extra sauce to prevent the noodles from drying out.

rice-white-with-tomatoes-and-or-tomato-b.title: White Rice with Tomatoes and/or Tomato-Based Sauce, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: This is boiled white rice prepared with tomatoes or a tomato‑based sauce and a modest amount of fat (oil or butter). The tomato component gives the dish a bright flavor and aroma, while the fat makes it more satisfying and helps absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
The rice‑tomato sauce combination is traditional in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Latin American cuisines.
Adding a small amount of fat enhances flavor and improves the absorption of lycopene from tomatoes.
White rice is a staple energy source in many cultures and often serves as a neutral base for more flavorful ingredients.
Tomato sauce can be made from fresh or canned tomatoes; both retain most of the nutrients.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides quick‑digesting carbohydrates that are readily converted to glucose, supporting energy levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C and lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes in the sauce supply vitamin C and lycopene, which support immunity and protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Improved nutrient absorption
items.content: Fat aids the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and carotenoids from the tomatoes.

items.title: Low sodium when homemade
items.content: Preparing the dish without excessive salt keeps sodium moderate, beneficial for blood pressure control.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: While rice contains modest protein, the combination with tomato sauce makes the meal more balanced.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or tomato juice.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Excessive added fat increases the calorie density of the dish and may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Additives in commercial sauce
items.content: When using ready‑made tomato sauces, check the label for added sugars, preservatives, or excess sodium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve as a side dish with meat, fish, or vegetable mains. Garnish with fresh herbs (basil, parsley) or spices (paprika, black pepper) to boost flavor. For extra protein, mix with beans or lentils.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. It can be frozen for up to 2 months after cooling and placed in a freezer‑safe bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain white roll is a soft bun made from whole‑grain wheat flour, baked without artificial colourings. It has a mild taste, a light bread aroma and a slightly sweet aftertaste. The roll is commonly used as a base for sandwiches, snacks and breakfasts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain flour retains the bran and germ, making the product more nutritious than refined white flour.
The white colour of the roll is achieved by using only wheat flour without added seeds or grains.
Traditionally popular in European cuisine, these rolls are often served with butter, cheese or ham.
Baked whole‑grain products have a longer shelf life due to lower moisture content.
Rolls are frequently chosen for diet plans because the fibre provides a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Rich in dietary fibre
items.content: Whole‑grain rolls contain fibre that supports normal bowel function and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They provide thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, which are essential for metabolism and energy production.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The roll supplies iron, magnesium and zinc, important for blood formation and immune health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white bread, whole‑grain rolls raise blood sugar more slowly.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Fibre and plant phytochemicals help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with gluten intolerance or wheat allergy may experience adverse reactions when consuming the roll.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some roll varieties contain added salt; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although less calorie‑dense than white bread, overeating can still lead to excess energy intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the roll fresh, split it open and spread butter, cream cheese or hummus. It works well for sandwiches with turkey, vegetables and greens, and makes a convenient breakfast base.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep rolls in an airtight bag at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate or freeze them wrapped in plastic to prevent drying out.

turnip-greens-frozen-cooked-fat-added.title: Turnip greens, frozen, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Turnip greens are the leafy tops of the turnip plant, a nutrient‑dense green vegetable. In this product the greens are blanched, quickly frozen, and later enriched with a small amount of fat to improve flavor and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turnip greens belong to the Brassicaceae family, the same as broccoli, kale and cabbage.
They are an excellent source of vitamins A, C, and K, as well as calcium and iron.
Turnip greens are traditional in Southern U.S. cooking and are also used in Asian stir‑fries.
Rapid freezing after harvest preserves most of the nutrients.
Adding a modest amount of fat helps the body absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements and gut health.

items.title: Improves mineral absorption
items.content: The added fat enhances the absorption of vitamins A and K.

items.title: Cruciferous vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to Brassicaceae plants.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed frozen greens can contain added salt; check the label if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Oxalate levels
items.content: High oxalate content may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen greens in a skillet with a little oil, stir‑fry them, add to soups or stews, or serve as a side dish with meat or fish. They can also be microwaved for 3‑4 minutes until hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product frozen at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, use within 1‑2 days and do not refreeze.
